title: Karmic tail 15-8-11 in the destiny matrix: physical aggression, the lion and a sword without scales

seo.title: Karmic tail 15-8-11, “Physical Aggression”, in the destiny matrix
seo.description: 15-8-11 is a tail about force that is sure it is right. A ten-second date check, why it holds both Strength and Justice, and where defence turns into violence.

short: 15-8-11 is the karmic tail that popular destiny matrix readings call “Physical Aggression”. Its scenario is force that is sure it is right. From the inside, the aggression of this tail almost never feels like aggression. It feels like justice: “he had it coming”, “I was only answering back”, “it’s the only language they understand”. The Devil (15) opens the circle: a flare-up, vehemence, a beast straining to break out. Strength (8) keeps the circle going: a hand on the lion’s jaws that can hold the beast back or let it loose — and then strength becomes violence. Justice (11) sits at the root: the sword and the scales. This tail always has the sword within reach; the task is to bring the scales back to it. So the main question of 15-8-11 is not “how do I stop getting angry” but how to make force serve measure, without measure becoming an excuse for force. And everyone with this tail has one more card at the centre of the matrix — the Emperor, a warrior with armour under his robe.

sections.h2: Do you have the 15-8-11 tail? A ten-second check
paragraphs: The tail depends entirely on the sum of the first three arcana of the matrix. 15-8-11 comes from one sum only, so the whole check comes down to one number.

ol: **Day arcanum** — your day of birth. If it is greater than 22, add its digits: 25 → 7, 29 → 11, 31 → 4.
**Year arcanum** — the sum of the digits of the year. If it comes out above 22, add the digits again: 1985 → 23 → 5, 1990 → 19, 2008 → 10.

paragraphs: Add the three numbers. **If you get exactly 29, you have 15-8-11.** Any other sum gives a different tail.

ul: 17.02.1990: 17 + 2 + 19 = 38 → not this one. It is 6-17-11: the root is also 11, but the tail is different.

paragraphs: Why this works. The tail is the three points of the bottom ray of the chart: M next to the centre, N in the middle, D in the bottom corner. The sum 29 reduces to 11 (2 + 9 = 11) — that is corner D. The centre of the chart, E, is the same sum plus D: 29 + 11 = 40 → 4. The tail’s entry M = D + E = 11 + 4 = 15, the middle N = D + M = 11 + 15 = 26 → 8. The sums 11, 38, 47 and 56 also put eleven in the corner, but they give a different centre, and the tail comes out as 6-17-11. There is no other way to 15-8-11 — this was checked by going through every day from 1900 to 2100.
15-8-11 is often confused with tails that share a card with it:

Tail
Centre of the chart
What it shares with 15-8-11

paragraphs: The same arithmetic yields a few facts you will rarely find anywhere else:

ul: **One person in 26 has it.** Among birth dates from 1940 to 2012, 15-8-11 comes up in 3.9% of cases — 11th place out of 26 possible tails. Together with the two other tails that begin with the Devil, it covers more than one person in five (22%).

**It hardly depends on the generation.** One in 23 among those born in the 1940s, one in 27 in the 1990s, one in 28 in the 2000s, one in 26 in the 2010s. Parents and children know this tail equally well.

**It appears in every year.** From 1900 to 2100 — between 8 and 21 dates a year. The most in years with the arcanum 15: among people alive today, those born in 1941 and 1950, with 21 dates each. The fewest in 2000, only eight dates, and they all lie on one diagonal: 15.12, 16.11, 17.10, 18.09, 19.08, 20.07, 21.06 and 22.05. Their day and month add up to 27.

**It has moved from spring to autumn.** Among people born in 1940–1999, there are twice as many spring dates with this tail as autumn ones. Among those born since 2000 it is the other way round: autumn dates outnumber spring ones, and there are two and a half times as many December dates as January ones. The reason is arithmetic. Years of the 20th century have a large arcanum (1990 → 19), so the day and month only have a little to add — the early months win. Years of the 21st century have a small arcanum (2008 → 10), and it is the late months that reach 29.

**11-8-15 is the same tail.** This scheme has no tail that begins with eleven: the first number of a tail, point M, is always a multiple of three — 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 or 21. If you see 11, 8 and 15 on the bottom ray of your chart, you are reading the same tail from the corner towards the centre. The roles don’t change: the Devil is the entry, eleven is the root.

paragraphs: Popular interpretations explain the name with a past-life legend. The soul supposedly had great physical strength and used it for evil: it was a cruel warrior or commander, took what it wanted by force, lashed out at those weaker than itself. In this life, the same readings say, the tail brings outbursts of anger, pressure and control at home and at work, and trouble with the law. Or the opposite plot — a childhood and a life next to someone else’s fist. The legend cannot be checked: numbers say nothing about past lives. But the name does not rest on the legend alone. It is written into the cards themselves.

Open Waite’s lists of divinatory meanings. The Devil’s list begins with “ravage, violence, vehemence, extraordinary efforts, force”. Strength has “power, energy, action, courage”, and reversed, “despotism, abuse of power”. Justice reversed has “bias, excessive severity”. The Emperor, who stands at the centre, has “stability, power, protection”, and also “authority and will”. The three cards of the tail and the card at the centre are four faces of force: violence, might, power and judgement. Waite even uses the same word for the Emperor and for Justice: “executive”.

The word “physical” is no accident either. Discussing old pictures of the Strength card, Waite cites the view that the figure on it represents “organic force, moral force and the principle of all force”. Organic means bodily: muscles, fists, height, voice. Among the meanings of Strength reversed, Benebell Wen lists “overreliance on the physical faculties rather than mental, emotional, intellectual, or spiritual”. That is physical aggression in the exact sense: the body answers where words, feelings or thought should have answered. The tail describes a path from organic force to moral force.

But the most important thing about the name is what it leaves out. The aggression of this tail does not come alone but together with being in the right. Discussing Justice reversed, Wen describes this almost word for word: “chauvinism, aggression, blind enthusiasm in a particular cause that may bring more harm than good, or actions that may be unjust rather than just”. And she adds that what drives a person to such actions is the feeling of having been treated unfairly. It is not malice that drives them but resentment at injustice. That is why 15-8-11 is the tail not of a villain but of a **judge with fists**.

sections.h2: The lion and the Devil are one beast
paragraphs: Wen notes that the lion on the Strength card recalls a line from the First Epistle of Peter: “Be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.” In the 15-8-11 tail these two cards stand side by side: the Devil at the entry, the lion in the middle. It is one and the same beast. Only one thing changes — whose hand rests on its jaws.

On Waite’s card, a woman is closing the lion’s jaws. Her “beneficent fortitude has already subdued the lion”, and it follows her on a chain of flowers. In one of its senses, Waite says, the lion signifies the passions, and Strength herself is “the higher nature in its liberation”. And Waite gives a detail that matters more for this tail than anything else: in the old engraving printed by Court de Gébelin, the woman is not closing the lion’s mouth but opening it. Closing is symbolically better, according to Waite, but both gestures convey mastery over the beast. The 15-8-11 tail is a constant choice between two gestures of one and the same hand.

Wen also writes about how to tame such a lion: not with brute force but with kindness and compassion. “The meek lamb will prevail over the open-mouthed lion.” She opens her description of the card with the words “Triumph of love over hate. Compassion is strength” and warns that you cannot use brute force to impose your will on others, only gentle, subtle influence.

The Devil has a fire of his own. Wen describes the picture in the Waite–Smith deck: the beast points its torch at the ground, and it looks as if it is setting the man’s tail on fire. The woman’s tail ends in fruit, the man’s in flame. The fire that on the Lovers card burned on the tree behind the man burns here on his tail. It is a ready-made image of anger as it is described from the inside: “they drove me to it”, “he was asking for it”. As if someone else had brought the fire. But the chained figures on this card, Waite writes, have human faces: their reason stays with them. And the one who towers above them is “not to be their master for ever”.

sections.h2: A sword without scales: how the circle works
paragraphs: Each card of this tail holds something in its hands that can strike or hold back. The Devil has a torch. Strength has bare hands on the lion’s jaws. Justice has a sword and scales. The Emperor at the centre has a sceptre, and armour under his robe. The tail describes what a person does with their strength at the moment they are sure they are right.

**1. Entry: the Devil — the flare-up.** The trigger can be anything: humiliation, someone’s insolence, disobedience from someone weaker, an encroachment on what is “mine” — a person, a place, a cause, one’s honour. What rises is what Waite calls vehemence. Wen sees in the Devil “a streak of hatred and resentment” and links the card with antagonism, despotism and enslavement. There is a lot of energy in the flare-up, and in itself it is not evil. The trouble is where it goes.
**2. Mechanism: Strength — the hand on the jaws.** From here on the eight decides everything, and it has two ways of failing. Wen describes both among the meanings of Strength reversed.

ul: **Brute force.** Answering with the body: hitting, shoving, gripping an arm harder than necessary, slamming a door so the plaster cracks, smashing a phone, blocking the way out, looming over someone. This also includes pressure without touching: shouting, threats, a fist raised “just like that”. This is the very failure Wen calls relying on the physical and being stubborn.

**Holding back with no outlet.** The person keeps the jaws shut with all their might: “I’m calm”, “everything’s fine” — and clenched teeth. Wen describes this Strength too: the person holds back, behaves too passively, and the lion overwhelms them. Suppressed anger doesn’t disappear. It builds up and breaks through later, out of nowhere, and most often on whoever is closest and weakest. Or it turns inwards: training to exhaustion, working yourself into the ground, risk-taking, punishing yourself.

paragraphs: Both failures are force without measure. One lets the beast out at once, the other later.

**3. Root: Justice — the sword and the scales.** Here is the key to the whole tail. The aggression of 15-8-11 almost always acquits itself: “he started it”, “I was defending myself”, “that’s how you raise children”, “nothing else gets through to him”. The person has the sword in their hand, while the scales are held in their head, and they always tip in their favour. Waite sees in Justice “the moral principle which deals unto every man according to his works”. In 1872 the German jurist Rudolf von Jhering said something about this image that lawyers have quoted ever since: **“The sword without the scales is brute force; the scales without the sword is the impotence of law.”** The root task of the tail is to bring the scales back to the sword.

Often the verdict is handed down before anything has happened. Psychologists call this hostile attribution: a person prone to aggression sees ill intent where there is none. Someone bumps into you in a crowd — “on purpose”. A message goes unanswered — “they’re ignoring me”. A child spills tea — “to spite me”. A meta-analysis of 41 studies of children and teenagers (Orobio de Castro and colleagues, 2002) showed that the stronger the habit of attributing hostility to others, the more aggressive the behaviour. The scales of this tail are broken from the start: one pan already holds the other person’s guilt.

**4. Repetition: two eyes for an eye.** Wen explains Justice through Newton’s third law: to every action there is always an equal and opposite reaction. Force gives rise to counter-force. In 2003 neuroscientists in London tested this almost literally. Two participants took turns pressing on each other’s finger through a special device. Each was asked to press back on the partner with exactly the force they had just felt — no more. Both tried honestly. And yet each turn came out on average 38% stronger than the one before. The reason lies in how the nervous system works: the brain feels its own pressing as weaker than someone else’s. The paper in the journal Science was called “Two eyes for an eye”. **Even an honest tit-for-tat answer escalates a fight, because your own blow always feels weaker than the one you received.**

“An eye for an eye” in ancient law, as historians often explain, was not a call for revenge but a limit on it: no more than an eye for an eye. Measure appeared in order to stop escalation. The 15-8-11 tail is escalation without measure. Every answer seems fair, and every one is a little stronger than the last. The circle closes like this: a flare-up, force, a justification, counter-force, a new flare-up. Between the turns come shame and the promise “never again”, which lasts until the next hurt.

sections.h2: Two numberings: what do you reach for first, the sword or the scales?
paragraphs: In the old Marseille order, Justice is eighth and Strength (La Force in French decks) eleventh. Waite swapped them. In his 1910 book he explained this in a single phrase — “for reasons which satisfy myself” — and added that the change means nothing to the reader. Wen writes that Waite never offered a public explanation for the switch, and that it goes back to the Cipher Manuscript, the founding document of the Order of the Golden Dawn. It is usually linked to the order’s astrology: Strength corresponds to Leo, Justice to Libra, and Leo comes before Libra in the zodiac. Most destiny matrix calculators and readings keep the Marseille order: 8 is Justice, 11 is Strength. This reading follows the cards of Waite’s deck.

In other tails that contain an eight or an eleven, the difference comes down to the name of one card. 15-8-11 is a special case: it contains both cards at once, and the numbering decides which of them keeps the circle going and which stands at the root.

head: Waite: the Devil → Strength → Justice

paragraphs: The two readings don’t contradict each other; they describe two sequences, and both are familiar from life. Some people hit first and then explain why there was no other way. Others spend a long time judging, collect evidence and pass sentence, and only then carry it out — with a fist, a raised voice or a cold punishment. The root is the same in both cases: the sword and the scales must work together. Strength without justice becomes violence. Justice without strength becomes rancour — an endless tally of grievances that will one day be presented with a fist anyway. Waite thought the swap meant nothing to the reader. For 15-8-11 it means one thing: what you reach for first. Recognise your own sequence — it will show you where to break the circle.

paragraphs: Many people with 15-8-11 recognise not one mode in themselves but several. For years — clenched teeth, then a flare-up, then shame, and clenched teeth again.

The least noticeable mode is **the Punisher**. This person sincerely doesn’t consider themselves aggressive: they never hit anyone without a reason, they punish for a reason. The belt “for a bad mark”, a week of icy silence “so he gets the message”, a public dressing-down “to keep order”, revenge on an ex-partner “in fairness”. There is always an explanation, and the explanation seems honest to them. This is the sword without scales in its purest form: the scales are there, but only the Punisher gets to use them.

**The Target** is the other side of the same tail. Popular readings mention it in passing, although it follows from the same triple just as directly. A person lives next to someone else’s aggression — a parent’s, a partner’s, a boss’s — and turns Justice against themselves: “I provoked him”, “it’s my own fault”, “but he always apologises afterwards”. Strength turns into endurance: putting up with things longer than anyone else would. Here the root task is the same — to bring the scales back. Only the honest verdict sounds different: the one who uses violence is responsible for it.

sections.h2: The hidden fourth card: everyone with 15-8-11 has the Emperor at the centre
paragraphs: Everyone with the 15-8-11 tail has 4, the Emperor, at the centre of the matrix. This is not a coincidence but arithmetic: the centre is always 4, and the method derives the tail’s entry from it. So the Devil of this tail is made of two cards: 15 = 11 + 4. In Waite’s numbering that is Justice plus the Emperor — righteousness plus power. In the calculators’ numbering it is Strength plus the Emperor — might plus power. What follows is our reading, not a rule of the method: the beast of this tail is made of power that is sure it is right.

Blaise Pascal described this mechanism back in the 17th century. “Justice without might is helpless; might without justice is tyrannical,” he writes in the Pensées. So the two must be combined: what is just must be made strong, or what is strong must be made just. Then comes a bitter twist. Justice is open to dispute; might is plain to see. And might, Pascal writes, gainsaid justice, called it unjust and declared itself just. “And thus being unable to make what is just strong, we have made what is strong just.” This is an exact description of the Devil in 15-8-11: force that has issued itself a judge’s mandate.

In the method, the centre of the chart is the comfort zone, the state a person returns to when nothing is asked of them. For this tail, the comfort zone is being in charge and being right at the same time. Deciding, protecting, keeping order: “my house, my rules”, “nobody treats me like that”, “hands off my people”. There is a lot that is good in this. In Waite’s divinatory list, the Emperor has not only power but also protection, aid and reason. At their best, such people are the first to step in between the bully and the one being bullied.

But the Emperor of the Waite–Smith deck wears armour under his red robe. Wen calls him a warrior king and writes that four is “the number of force and sovereignty”. In a conflict, she says, the card stands for jus ad bellum, the right to wage war: your cause is just. And straight away she asks a question that should make the heart of anyone with 15-8-11 skip a beat: what is your dominion? What have you conquered? Behind the Emperor’s throne is a dry canyon. The kingdom is parched. In one kind of spread Wen reads this card as too belligerent an approach and **“scorching the earth in a desperate effort to wield control”**. Winning the argument and being left in a house where nobody talks to you any more — that is exactly the scorched earth.

The same Waite offers a hint for the way out. In its highest sense, his Emperor is “the lordship of thought rather than of the animal world”. That is exactly what the 15-8-11 tail needs: not to give up power and strength, but to set thought above the Devil’s beast. The tail’s path runs from the centre to the root, from the Emperor to Justice. The Emperor decides: “I’m right here because I’m in charge here.” Justice asks: would the scales agree with this decision if someone other than you were holding them? Wen stresses that Justice is human justice, not divine: the laws of people and a decision made fairly and impartially. An Emperor who wants to become just stops being his own plaintiff, judge and executioner.

sections.h2: The tail in a mirror: where else 15, 8 and 11 appear in your chart
paragraphs: The 15-8-11 triple appears in the matrix not only on the bottom ray. Going through every date from 1900 to 2100 shows where else it stands and what all holders of the tail have in common.

**The relationship line always begins with the Devil.** Point M, the tail’s entry, is shared in the method with the relationship line M–R1–R. So for everyone with 15-8-11, the relationship programme also opens with the fifteenth arcanum. And for those born in years with the arcanum 10 — 1999, 2008, 2017 and 2026 — the relationship line repeats the tail in full: 15-8-11. Among people alive today, these are only young adults, teenagers and children: 17 dates in each of these years. For them the scenario is written into the chart twice: as the old circle and as the way they build closeness. Our reading: for them the rules of arguing as a couple are no small thing but the main work with the tail.

**For those born in November, the tail is reflected in a mirror.** The number of the month stands on the top ray of the chart, at the start of the talent line. November holders of 15-8-11 have eleven there, and the talent line comes out as 11-8-15. These are the same three cards, placed the same way as below: eleven at the outer corner, the Devil next to the centre. What follows is our reading: for these people the trap and the gift are made of the same material. What has to be tamed in the tail becomes, in the talent, the ability to understand conflict, strength and justice from the inside. Such people grow into those who can stop a fight — because they know how one starts.

**All three numbers of the tail live in the lower chakras.** In the matrix’s chakra table, everyone with 15-8-11 has eleven in Muladhara and the Devil in Svadhisthana (both in the energy column), while Manipura is the same for everyone: 4-4-8, the Emperor twice and Strength in the emotions column. In the method, Muladhara stands for the body and support, Svadhisthana for joy and creativity, Manipura for will and status. People born in 1941 and 1950 have all three cards in Muladhara alone: 15, 11 and 8. Our reading: the 15-8-11 tail lives on the ground floor — in the body, desire and will. That is why it is physical: anger here first clenches the fist and the jaw, and only later becomes a thought. And Strength in the emotions of Manipura hints at where this tail’s real power lies — not in the armour but in the hand that knows how to keep the jaws closed.
The scenes below are made-up examples, not a description of everyone with this tail.

**Master of the house.** Here the Emperor from the centre is at work. Order is set up in the family, and that order rests on fear: “as long as you live under my roof”, “I said so”. Jealousy looks like a property right: “you’re mine”, “he’s mine”. The Devil puts on the Emperor’s armour, and control is called care. Physical aggression in such a home doesn’t necessarily go as far as a blow. A fist driven into the wall next to someone’s head, a smashed plate, a blocked doorway, an arm gripped too hard — that is the language of force too, and everyone in the house understands it.

**An argument as a trial.** The second plot is the “verdict first” one. The person collects evidence, keeps a tally of grievances, then presents the charge and carries out the sentence on the spot. The punishment can come without hands: icy silence, cutting off money, “if that’s how it is, you’re nothing to me”. Justice is at work here, but only one side holds the scales.

**Next to someone else’s fist.** The third plot is the Target mode. A partner or parent lashes out, and the person with 15-8-11 explains, endures and finds the fault in themselves. Strength has gone into endurance; the scales weigh only one’s own guilt.

The strong version in all three plots is **rules for conflict**. A couple agrees in advance: hands — never; not in front of the children; not at night and not when drunk; whoever says “stop” gets a pause, and the conversation resumes when both have cooled down. The Emperor at his best knows how to write laws. Here he has to write one for himself.

The strong side here is real. Capacity for work, endurance, a love of competition, courage in conflict. People with 15-8-11 are not afraid of difficult conversations, they stand up for their own people and hold up well in a crisis when others are at a loss.

The shadow is just as visible. Managing through fear: a public dressing-down “to keep order”, “I’m tough but fair”, shouting as a work tool. A war “on principle” that costs more than the thing being fought over. Lawsuits, claims, litigation — Waite’s Justice reversed has “law in all its departments, legal complications”. And conflicts with the law itself, when people try to “restore justice” with their own hands.

Things go well where force is subordinated to rules in advance. Sport and coaching, rescue services, security, service with a clear code, law and mediation, crisis management, heavy physical work, protecting those who cannot protect themselves. These are examples, not a list of “correct professions”. And a uniform does not cure the tail by itself: in uniform the circle turns just the same if the sword has no scales.

The most dangerous family formula for this tail is “I was hit as a kid, and I turned out fine”. Research says otherwise. A meta-analysis of 75 studies spanning fifty years and more than 160,000 children (Gershoff and Grogan-Kaylor, 2016) showed that the more often a child is spanked, the higher their aggression and antisocial behaviour. Force used to “teach” teaches force above all. Someone who learned in childhood that the stronger one is right easily confuses strength with being right as an adult.

A parent with 15-8-11 should test every punishment with three questions from Justice. Is it proportionate? Was it decided at the peak of anger or afterwards? Would I accept such a punishment from someone stronger than me, for the same fault? And one rule from the root of the tail: don’t punish while you are angry. A punishment decided in anger is a flare-up, not upbringing.

sections.h2: Defence or attack: how to tell them apart

ul: Did you need force to stop a danger — or to punish?
Did you stop when the danger was over — or when you ran out of steam?
Would you agree to someone stronger than you treating you the same way for the same reason?
Who passed the verdict — only you? Would an outsider who heard both sides agree with it?
Do you want the damage made good — or the other person to hurt just as much?
Is your answer proportionate — or meant “to teach them a lesson”?
Are you protecting what is yours — or controlling what is someone else’s: another person’s time, body, phone, decisions?
Does your “you mustn’t” apply to you as well?
Can the other person say “no” to you — without anything happening to them for it?

paragraphs: **Calm or clenched teeth:**

ul: Does the anger pass — or wait for a convenient moment?
Do you lash out at those stronger than you — or at those who are weaker and depend on you?
After “I’m calm”, does your body relax — or do your jaws stay clenched?

sections.h2: What to do with the 15-8-11 tail: eight practices
paragraphs: These are the author’s exercises, drawn from the logic of the triple — not a ritual and not a promise of results. Each one targets its own link in the circle.

ol: **A hand on the jaws.** Learn your early signals: the jaw tightens, the fists grow heavy, the face gets hot, the voice rises, the world narrows to one person. This is the moment when the hand is still on the lion’s jaws. At the very first signal — pause: leave the room, breathe slowly, take a walk. A 2024 meta-analysis of 154 studies with more than 10,000 participants showed that anger and aggression are reduced precisely by calming activities: slow breathing, muscle relaxation, taking a break, calm movement. “Letting off steam”, on the other hand, does not help. In a well-known experiment by Brad Bushman, people who hit a punchbag while thinking about the person who had provoked them were angrier afterwards, and behaved more aggressively, than those who did nothing at all.

**The verdict — tomorrow.** In this tail one person plays four roles at once: victim, prosecutor, judge and executioner. Separate them in time. Today you are the victim — you are allowed to be angry. Tomorrow you are the judge — you decide what is proportionate. The sentence is carried out only by lawful means: a conversation, a boundary, an agreement, a formal complaint, a court. On the card, Justice is seated, not running.

**Someone else’s scales.** Your own blow always feels weaker than the one you received — the “Two eyes for an eye” experiment showed that. So measuring your answer by your own sense of it is pointless. Before you respond, ask someone with no stake in it: “Is this proportionate?” And if there is nobody to ask, answer half a tone softer than seems fair. This is not weakness but a correction for the way perception works.

**“No” while it is still a word.** Rage builds up where boundaries are defended too late. A person puts up with things, puts up with them, and then explodes — and ends up in the wrong. Say “this doesn’t work for me” the first time, not the twentieth. A small early “no” spares you a big late fist.

**Work for the lion.** The body of this tail needs strength — give it a place with rules. Martial arts with a coach and the etiquette of the dojo: a 2017 meta-analysis of studies with children and teenagers showed that such training reduces their aggression. Team ball games, heavy physical work. In judo, the first thing a beginner learns is how to fall — it is called ukemi. Learning to lose without rage is the best training for 15-8-11. What matters is that it is a regular part of the body’s life, not a release after a fight.

**A code of strength.** Write down the rules for your own strength. When I may use it: to stop a danger, to protect someone weaker. When never: against those who depend on me — children, a partner, subordinates, animals; when I have been drinking; in the middle of a late-night argument. What I do instead of hitting. Codes of chivalry, the rules of sport, military regulations — force has always been tamed by written rules. The Emperor at the centre of your chart knows how to write laws. Let him write one for himself.

**Close old cases.** Make a list of the grievances you still carry. Next to each, write: who, what, what would be fair now, and whether it is achievable. If it is, pursue it by lawful means. If not, close the case. You don’t have to forgive, but stop running the trial in your head. Unclosed cases are fuel for the next flare-up.

**If the force is aimed at you.** This is not karma and not a deserved sentence. If you are in danger, call your local emergency number or a local crisis line; children can reach out, and so can parents. Many cities have crisis centres for people facing violence. And if you yourself can’t stop, turn to a psychologist or an anger management programme. These are exactly the outside scales the tail is missing.

sections.h2: The strong side of 15-8-11: a defender with a sword and scales
paragraphs: In its worked-through version this tail gives a rare combination. The person knows their strength and isn’t afraid of it (the Devil), knows how to hold it (Strength) and subordinates it to measure (Justice). They don’t look away in a conflict, and yet they don’t escalate it. People come to them when someone is needed to stand in the doorway: to protect, to stop, to judge fairly. In a fight it is people like this who are listened to, because everyone understands: this person could hit — and doesn’t.

In Waite’s divinatory list for Strength there is a word that describes a worked-through 15-8-11 more precisely than any other — magnanimity. It is the virtue of the strong: it begins where you could crush someone and don’t. The Emperor’s list has protection. Justice has rightness and probity. Together they add up to the image for which this tail, if you see it as a task, exists: strength in the service of justice, not justice in the service of strength.

Waite ends his description of the Devil with a promise: the one who towers over the chained pair is “not to be their master for ever”. And of the woman on the Strength card he writes that her beneficent fortitude has already subdued the lion. The 15-8-11 tail is a path from one to the other: from the beast that sets things on fire to the hand that holds. The sword stays a sword. The scales appear beside it.

sections.h2: What this reading is based on

ul: **Calculation** — Natalia Ladini’s classic destiny matrix scheme with points A–T: D = A + B + C, E = A + B + C + D, M = D + E, N = D + M; every sum over 22 is reduced by adding its digits. All numerical facts in the article — the single sum 29, the constant centre 4, frequencies by generation, year and month, the matches with the relationship and talent lines, the constant numbers in the chakras — come from going through every date from 1900 to 2100. Shares were calculated over dates from 1940 to 2012, by decade and over dates since 2000.

**Card meanings** — A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, reissued 1922) and Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015). Quotations are given in the authors’ original English. Card numbering follows Waite: VIII is Strength, XI is Justice. The remarks on the Golden Dawn’s Cipher Manuscript follow Wen’s note. The Bible verse is quoted as Wen gives it, from the English Standard Version.

**Quotations** — Rudolf von Jhering, The Struggle for Law (1872); Blaise Pascal, Pensées, the fragment “Justice, might” (298 in Brunschvicg’s numbering), quoted in W. F. Trotter’s English translation.

**Research** — S. Shergill, P. Bays, C. Frith, D. Wolpert, “Two eyes for an eye: the neuroscience of force escalation”, Science, 2003; B. Orobio de Castro et al., meta-analysis of hostile attribution, Child Development, 2002; B. Bushman, “Does venting anger feed or extinguish the flame?”, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 2002; S. Kjærvik, B. Bushman, meta-analysis of anger management methods, Clinical Psychology Review, 2024; A. Harwood, M. Lavidor, Y. Rassovsky, meta-analysis of martial arts and aggression in children and adolescents, Aggression and Violent Behavior, 2017; E. Gershoff, A. Grogan-Kaylor, meta-analysis of corporal punishment, Journal of Family Psychology, 2016.

**The name “Physical Aggression” and the past-life legend** come from popular interpretations of the destiny matrix. Neither Waite nor Wen wrote about the matrix or karmic tails: putting the three cards together into a scenario, the reading of the centre, of the two numberings, of the mirror matches and of the chakras are the author’s interpretation.

This is an esoteric model for self-observation, not a forecast and not a substitute for professional help. If there is violence or threats in your life, or you cannot cope with your own anger, the tail is not the cause: what is needed here is real help, not work with numbers.

faq.q: What happened in the past life of a person with the 15-8-11 tail?
faq.a: Popular interpretations say the person had great physical strength and used it for evil: they were a cruel warrior or commander, took what belonged to others by force, tormented those weaker than themselves. Less often, that they themselves were a victim of violence. This is a legend of the tradition: neither numbers nor cards establish events in past lives. It is more useful to read it as a question the tail asks in this life: whose side is my strength on — the one who protects, or the one who punishes?

faq.q: Does 15-8-11 mean I’m aggressive, or that I’ll be beaten?
faq.a: No. The tail predicts neither violence nor fights nor any events at all. It describes a way of handling anger, strength and a sense of justice that can repeat itself. Among Waite’s meanings for the Devil there is an important proviso: “that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil”. Wen adds that this card does not necessarily mean the person is entirely to blame. Many people with 15-8-11 have never hit anyone. Their tail shows up as restraint through clenched teeth, as a heightened sense of justice, or as work that involves protecting others. If there is violence in your life, on either side, the numbers are not the cause, and the help you need is real help.

faq.q: Why is 8 Strength in one calculator and Justice in another?
faq.a: These are two numberings of the deck. In the old Marseille order and in most matrix calculators, the eighth card is Justice and the eleventh Strength. Waite swapped them, and in his deck the eighth is Strength. The tail itself doesn’t change: the numbers are the same. But 15-8-11 contains both cards, so the numbering decides which of them keeps the circle going and which stands at the root. Both readings are covered in the “Two numberings” section above.

Yes, if 11, 8 and 15 stand on the bottom ray of your chart: you have simply read the tail from the outer corner towards the centre. In the calculation it is written from the inner point M to the corner D, and M is always a multiple of three, so there is no tail that begins with eleven. The roles don’t change: 15 is the entry, 11 is the root. But 11-8-15 also appears on the top ray — in the talent line of holders of the tail born in November. There it is no longer the tail but its mirror image.

faq.q: Are the 15-8-11 tail and the “15-8-11 programme” in relationships the same thing?
faq.a: The karmic tail is only the triple on the bottom ray, between the centre and the bottom corner of the chart. The same numbers appear on the relationship line M–R1–R for all holders of the tail born in 1999, 2008, 2017 and 2026. There the triple describes not an old scenario but how you build closeness: the entry through passion, the mechanism through strength, the outcome through measure. And in the compatibility matrix the numbers are calculated from two dates, so the same triple describes the scenario of the couple. If 15-8-11 appears in several places in your chart, the practices in this article apply to all of them.

It shares its entry, the Devil, with 15-5-8 and 15-20-5. But in 15-5-8 the pull is covered by the Hierophant’s rule; that is a tail about a double life. In 15-20-5 the pull is judged by Judgement; that is a tail about rebelling against “how things should be”. In 15-8-11 the Devil is no longer a pull but a flare-up, and it is met by strength: the question is who holds the sword. With 6-17-11 it shares its root, eleven, but the entry is different — the Lovers: there measure is needed by choice and dreams, not by force. With 6-8-20 it shares its middle, Strength, and the same centre, the Emperor, but the entry and root are different: there strength goes into enduring what was never chosen.

faq.q: Is 15-8-11 different for women and men?
faq.a: No. Gender plays no part in the calculation, and the meaning of the tail doesn’t depend on it. Popular readings like to give men the fists and women the role of victim or “making scenes”, but these are stereotypes, not arithmetic. A woman with 15-8-11 can be both the Flare-up and the Punisher. A man can be the Target. Most often it is one and the same person in different years of life.

There are plenty of such children: among people born since 2000, about one in 27 has 15-8-11. Often this is a child with a sharp sense of justice, for whom “that’s not fair!” is the main trigger. It helps if the adults don’t answer force with force but give the child words for anger: “you’re angry because nobody listened to you”. If family decisions are explained, and the child’s side is heard first and the decision made afterwards. If they have a sport with a coach and rules, where strength can be spent fairly. And if they are taught that the strong protect rather than punish. Children born in 2008 and 2017 also have the 15-8-11 triple on their relationship line — for them family rules for arguments matter especially.

The numbers in the matrix don’t change — what changes is how the scenario plays out. Signs of a worked-through tail: you notice your anger before it reaches your hands; your answers are proportionate, and you check them through someone else’s eyes; punishment is not decided at the peak of anger; you defend your boundaries with words and in time, not with fists and too late; old cases are closed. And most important: people feel calm around you, not afraid.

intro: If your calculator calls eight Justice and eleven Strength, it is the same tail. 15-8-11 contains both cards at once, and the two numberings of the deck swap them round. Both readings are covered below.

head: Position
Arcanum
Role in the scenario
Image
rows: the flare-up: anger, hurt, the right to “hit back”
the torch with which the beast sets a man’s tail alight
the strength that holds the beast or lets it loose
a hand on the lion’s jaws
measure: a proportionate answer instead of retribution
stands in every chart with this tail: power, protection, “I decide here”

report: The legend of 15-8-11 reads like a guilty verdict. In a past life, the story goes, the soul had great physical strength and used it for evil: a cruel warrior who took what it wanted by force and lashed out at anyone weaker. Hence the name popular readings give the tail — “Physical Aggression”. The legend cannot be checked: numbers say nothing about past lives. But the name rests on more than a legend. It is written into the cards themselves.

Waite’s divinatory meanings for the Devil open with “ravage, violence, vehemence, extraordinary efforts, force”. Strength reversed has “despotism, abuse of power”. Justice reversed, “bias, excessive severity”. The Emperor, who stands at the centre of the matrix for everyone with this tail, has “stability, power, protection”. Four cards, four faces of force: violence, might, power and judgement. Waite even calls both the Emperor and Justice by one word: “executive”.

But what matters most in the name is what it leaves out. This tail’s aggression arrives together with righteousness. Discussing Justice reversed, Benebell Wen describes it almost word for word: “chauvinism, aggression, blind enthusiasm in a particular cause that may bring more harm than good, or actions that may be unjust rather than just”. Such actions, she writes, are prompted by a feeling that what happened was not fair. From the inside it sounds like “he had it coming”, “I was only answering back”, “it’s the only language they understand”. So 15-8-11 is the tail not of a villain but of a **judge with fists**.

report.h3: The lion and the Devil are one beast

report: Wen notes that the lion of Strength recalls a line from 1 Peter: “the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour”. In this tail the two cards stand side by side: the Devil at the entry, Strength in the middle. The beast is the same; only the hand on its jaws changes. On Waite’s card a woman closes the lion’s mouth, but he also cites an older engraving printed by Court de Gébelin, in which she opens it. Both gestures, Waite says, convey mastery over the beast. 15-8-11 is a constant choice between two gestures of the same hand.

The hand can fail in two ways. Brute force: shoving, gripping harder than necessary, blocking the way out, driving a fist into the wall next to someone’s head. And holding back with no outlet: “I’m calm” through clenched jaws, until the anger breaks through out of nowhere — on whoever is closest and weakest, or on oneself. **Both failures are force without measure. One lets the beast out at once, the other later.**

report.h3: A blow always feels lighter to the hand that throws it

report: The least visible mode of the tail is the Punisher, who never hits without cause and only punishes what was earned: the belt “for a bad mark”, a week of icy silence “so he gets the message”, a public dressing-down “to keep order”. The sword is in the hand, the scales in the head, and only the Punisher does the weighing.

And bias is only part of it. In 2003, neuroscientists in London asked two participants to take turns pressing on each other’s finger — with exactly the force each had just felt. Both tried honestly, and yet each turn came out 38% stronger on average than the last: the brain feels its own push as weaker than another’s. The paper in Science was called “Two eyes for an eye”. **Even an honest tit-for-tat escalates a fight.**

The circle closes like this: a flare-up, force, a justification, counter-force, a new flare-up. Between the turns come shame and the promise “never again”, which lasts until the next hurt. In 1872 the jurist Rudolf von Jhering said of the image of Justice: “The sword without the scales is brute force; the scales without the sword is the impotence of law.”

The Emperor at the centre of the matrix is no coincidence but the arithmetic of the method: this tail’s Devil is made of two cards, 15 = 11 + 4. Justice plus the Emperor — righteousness plus power. From here on, our reading: the beast of 15-8-11 is made of power that is sure it is right. Blaise Pascal described this mechanism in the 17th century: justice is open to dispute, might is plain to see, and might declared itself just. “And thus being unable to make what is just strong, we have made what is strong just.”

At his best, the Emperor is the first to step between the bully and the bullied. Wen calls him a warrior king: in a conflict, his card stands for jus ad bellum, the right to wage war — the cause is just. But in one kind of spread she also sees in him **“scorching the earth in a desperate effort to wield control”**. Winning the argument and living on in a house where nobody talks to the winner — that is the scorched earth.

The Emperor decides: “I’m right here because I’m in charge here.” Justice asks whether the scales would agree with the decision if someone else were holding them. The tail’s path runs from the first voice to the second:

ul: Catch the early signals — a clenched jaw, a hot face, a world narrowed to one person — and pause at the first: leave, breathe slowly, walk. “Letting off steam” does not help: in Brad Bushman’s experiment, people who hit a punchbag while thinking of whoever had provoked them were later more aggressive than those who did nothing.

Pass the verdict tomorrow. In this tail one person plays four roles: victim, prosecutor, judge and executioner. Today, be angry; tomorrow, decide what is proportionate; carry out the sentence only with words, a boundary, an agreement or the courts. No punishment at the height of anger.

Borrow someone else’s scales: ask a person with no stake in it whether the response is proportionate. If there is nobody to ask, answer half a tone softer than seems fair. This is a correction for perception, not weakness.
Say “no” while it is still a word. A small, early “no” heads off a big, late fist.

report: The tail has a flip side too — life next to someone else’s fist, when the scales weigh only one’s own guilt: “I provoked him”, “it’s my own fault”. The honest verdict is different: this is neither karma nor deserved punishment; whoever uses violence answers for it. In danger, call a local emergency number or crisis line. And for anyone who cannot stop on their own, there is a psychologist or an anger management programme — the very outside scales the tail lacks.

In the worked-through version, a person knows their strength without fearing it, can hold it and submits it to measure. Such people are called when someone must stand in the doorway: to protect, to stop, to judge fairly. They are heeded because everyone understands: **this person could hit — and doesn’t.**

For a worked-through 15-8-11, Waite’s list for Strength has an exact word — magnanimity, the virtue of the strong: it begins where someone could crush another and doesn’t. And Waite ends his description of the Devil with a promise: the one exalted above the chained figures “is not to be their master for ever”. The sword stays a sword. The scales appear beside it.
